newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - UK's Brown offers fresh start to EU ministers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK's Brown offers fresh start to EU ministers.

text.p: In his first outing with fellow European Union finance ministers, Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, Gordon Brown, arrived on Monday ready to make clear the new Labour government's position on a wide range of issues.
Although little change is anticipated from the ousted Tory government's stance on Europe's planned single currency, Brown is expected to argue for a cut in EU taxes on energy.
EU finance ministers will get an update on the European Commission's proposals to harmonise EU energy taxes with a view to extending taxation to all energy products by 2002.

In a glimpse of Britain's readiness to engage its European partners more constructively, Brown arrived at 0630 GMT to meet EU Commission president Jacques Santer and Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy.

Rather than arrive through the customary back entrance for diplomats, Brown surprised a handful of awaiting journalists by coming through the front door of the EU's ministerial headquarters, offering only a polite smile.

After his decision to give the Bank of England greater latitude in setting monetary policy, Brown is seen extending the former government's wait-and-see approach towards economic and monetary union (EMU) despite last week's rumours that Britain might re-enter Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism.
EU finance ministers will also review the fiscal situation across the 15-nation bloc, giving both Finland and the Netherlands high marks for their budget-slashing efforts.

Both countries will be taken off the list of governments with so-called excessive deficits, joining Luxembourg, Ireland and Denmark, the only countries currently in line with the Maastricht Treaty's requirements for deficits and debt.

Governments wishing to qualify for EMU must bring their 1997 deficits down to three percent of Gross Domestic Product. They must also show public debt falling to 60 percent of GDP at a satisfactory pace.

Italy, incensed by a recent Commission forecast showing that its 1997 deficit would settle just above the Maastricht target, is expected to receive a terse warning that it must do more to rein in expenditure.
An Italian newspaper on Sunday said the warning to Italy, given to all governments with excessive deficits, would be "the most severe."
EU ministers will also review the economic convergence programmes of Spain and Portugal, two countries struggling to qualify for the single currency in 1999.
